                      matchday injuries, the authors noted several important correlations. They found that the
                      number of training injuries was positively related to greater upper body reactance, whereas
                      increased reactance in the right lower limb was associated with shorter injury duration.
                      Furthermore, in match players, they found that the number of injuries sustained was
                      negatively related to higher reactance in the right upper limb, perhaps indicating that body
                      composition metrics can provide a better indicator of injury risk. Their findings suggest
                      that BIVA might be a key method for the evaluation of injury risk and performance, hence
                      there is a need for further studies to establish this.
                           Considering that no studies on dietary supplements were submitted to this Special
                      Issue, we would like to highlight several key factors that we believe are important for
                      the research community and practitioners. Nutritional supplements are commercially
                      available products characterized by containing a nutrient or dietary ingredient formu-
                      lated to complement the diet in populations with special needs or specific goals. These
                      ingredients can include vitamins, amino acids and their derivatives, minerals, or glan-
                      dular extracts, herbs, or other plants in commercial forms such as tablets, soft gels, gel
                      capsules, liquids, or powders that are taken orally. In 1994, the United States approved
                      the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (https://www.congress.gov/bill/10
                      3rd-congress/senate-bill/784, accessed on 29 July 2024), which classifies supplements in a
                      special category of “foods”. In Europe, Directive 2002/46/EC from the European Parlia-
                      ment (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/46/2024-02-06, accessed on 29 July 2024)
                      established guidelines regarding food supplements.
                           Unfortunately, misinformation accelerated by influencers and YouTubers without
                      training in human nutrition and unethical practices by certain brands, the use of low-
                      quality raw materials to cut costs, and high commercial demand have created a landscape
                      prone to various issues in the supplement industry, but even when valid, misuse could lead
                      to considerable sides effects [1]. Sports supplements are now added to athletes’ regular diets
                      to enhance energy availability during physical exertion, accelerate post-exercise recovery
                      processes, and generally improve physical performance [2,3]. However, attention must also
                      be paid to misinterpretation by nutrition professionals who apply classification systems
                      designed exclusively for high-performance athletes (such as the ABCD system from the
                      Australian Institute of Sport) to physically active individuals who attend fitness centers
                      for esthetic or health reasons. In this regard, we encourage practitioners to use the ABC
                      categorization system proposed by the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN),
                      which is also based on the quality and quantity of scientific support available for both
                      the athletic and recreationally active population [3]. For tactical populations, the military
                      community, healthcare providers, and Department of Defense civilians should consider and
                      promote the “Operation Supplement Safety” program (https://www.opss.org/, accessed
                      on 20 August 2024).
                           Recently, some authors have introduced the framework Food First but Not Always
                      Food Only (FFNFO), which highlights seven special scenarios for the responsible use of
                      supplements [4]:
                      •    Some nutrients are difficult to obtain in sufficient amounts from the diet or may require
                           excessive energy intake and/or the consumption of other nutrients.
                      •    Some nutrients are abundant only in foods that athletes do not eat or do not like.
                      •    The nutrient content of certain foods with established ergogenic benefits is highly variable.
                      •    Concentrated doses of certain nutrients are needed to correct deficiencies and/or
                           promote immune tolerance.
                      •    Some foods may be difficult to consume before, during, or immediately after exercise.
                      •    Supplements certified by third-party organizations (e.g., NSF, BSCG, Informed Sport,
                           etc.) could help where there are concerns about food hygiene or contamination [4].
                          It has been shown that various supplements may contain contaminants that are
                      unethically not disclosed on the nutrition label. This gives rise to the concept of contami-
                      nant supplementation, where there is a risk both to health and of positive doping results
                      due to the inadvertent consumption of substances prohibited by the World Anti-Doping
 Life 2024, 14, 1392                                                                                                   3 of 4



                      Agency [5]. Contamination can occur for several reasons, whether accidental or intentional,
                      including (i) the presence of contaminants in the raw materials and a low-quality manufac-
                      turing process (such as the sharing of materials during production or inadequate cleaning),
                      (ii) alterations during transportation (including packaging and storage), (iii) fraudulent
                      labels indicating undisclosed ingredients or different quantities, and (iv) deliberate contam-
                      ination to enhance efficacy [6].
                             Among the common contaminants reported in the scientific literature are anabolic andro-
                      genic steroids, sibutramine, clenbuterol, hormonal peptides, methylhexanamine, endocrine
                      disruptors, and higenamine, along with various molecules that have not yet been chemically
                      described [7,8]. It is important to highlight that the minimum required performance levels
                      of these substances are extremely low, which increases the risk. For example, the limits
                      vary between 0.4 and 2.5 ng/mL for anabolic androgenic steroids (https://www.wada-
                      ama.org/sites/default/files/resources/files/td2022mrpl_v1.0_final_eng.pdf, accessed on
                      29 July 2024). These sources of accidental or intentional contamination in supplements
                      are verified through quantitative chemical analysis using high-performance liquid chro-
                      matography coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS), which allows for the analysis
                      of the athletes’ exposome [9]. Generally, products with a higher risk of contamination
                      include fat burners, mass gainers, testosterone boosters, herbal extracts, and others that use
                      proprietary blends [10]. These products are currently the most associated with reports of
                      fraud and deception online [11,12].
                             Since several contamination cases from supplements and food products have been
                      reported among athletes across various sports disciplines [13], it is crucial to implement
                      rigorous control measures. First, it is essential to assess whether the use of a supplement is
                      necessary, following the FFNFO framework. Verifying the target populations for which sup-
                      plement classification systems are intended is recommended. Additionally, it is important
                      to choose brands certified by third-party organizations (e.g., NSF, BSCG, Informed-Sport,
                      Cologne List), which verify the identity, quality, and quantity of ingredients. When appli-
                      cable, these organizations also verify the freshness (for liquid oils) and disintegration (for
                      tablets) of the supplements [14].
                             Researchers and professionals are encouraged to read the Strategic Plan for 2025–2029
                      from the Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS) of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in
                      the United States, as the Dietary Supplements Research Coordinating Committee (DSRCC)
                      has been established to promote collaboration and the coordination of research and training
                      activities on supplements (https://ods.od.nih.gov/About/NIHDSRCC.aspx, accessed on
                      29 July 2024). In Europe, it is recommended to closely follow the publications and news
                      from the European Food Safety Authority (https://www.efsa.europa.eu/es, accessed on
                      29 July 2024). Likewise, consumers are encouraged to report adverse effects associated with
                      supplement use on the platforms provided by each governmental regulatory entity (FDA in
                      the US, INVIMA in Colombia, COFEPRIS in Mexico, ANMAT in Argentina, AECOSAN in
                      Spain, etc.). Finally, healthcare professionals and consumers in general can take advantage
                      of free access to original dietary supplement labels to seek products with high-quality raw
                      materials and third-party seals by consulting the NIH dietary supplement label database
                      (https://dsld.od.nih.gov/, accessed on 20 August 2024).
                             It is crucial to ensure that professional work is based on scientific evidence, and
                      therefore, continuous research in sports nutrition should be promoted to provide practical
                      recommendations for dietary supplements that demonstrate efficacy and safety [15]. As
                      editors of high-impact scientific journals, we invite the scientific community to submit
                      their work in the research areas described in this Editorial, following the recommendations
                      outlined in the PRESENT and PERSiST guidelines as extensions of CONSORT and PRISMA
                      for clinical trials and systematic reviews with meta-analyses in sports nutrition, respectively.

                      J.L.P.; writing—review and editing, R.B.K. and R.C. All authors have read and agreed to the published
                      version of the manuscript.

12	Sports injuries and game stakes: Concussions in the
13	National Football League
14	
15	Pascal Courty1,2 | Jeffrey Cisyk3
16	
17	1
18	 University of Victoria, Victoria, British
19	Columbia, Canada                                         Abstract
20	2
21	CEPR, London, UK                                         The National Football League's regular‐season games are not of equal
22	3
23	 Charles River Associates, Chicago,                      importance: some games loom larger than others for determining a team's
24	Illinois, USA                                            chance to qualify for the playoffs. We develop an incentive‐based measure of
25	Correspondence
26	                                                         the impact of winning a game on a team's qualification probability to study the
27	Pascal Courty.                                           relationship between stakes and injuries. We find teams are 24 percentage
28	Email: pcourty@uvic.ca                                   points more likely to suffer concussions in games where a win secures one
29	                                                         team a playoff berth. This is the first evidence to support the risk‐escalation
30	                                                         hypothesis that injuries increase with a competition's stakes. We then
31	                                                         discuss implications for sports injury prevention.
32	
33	                                                         KEYWORDS
34	                                                         concussion, incentive, injury policy, injury prevention, National Football League, risk‐
35	                                                         escalation, sports injury

43	1 | INTRODUCTION
44	
45	Sports injuries are a major concern to athletes, medical experts, and policy makers. Scholars in sports medicine and
46	sports management have made multiple proposals to minimize the injury cost of participating in sport, such as pre-
47	vention, treatment, protective equipment mandate, or changes to a sport's rules (Finch, 2006). This existing approach
48	tends to view injuries as unfortunate yet largely unavoidable accidents.
49	    In this work, we investigate whether some sports injuries occur because athletes take risk in the pursuit of the
50	pinnacle of success. According to the risk‐escalation hypothesis, injuries should be more prevalent as competition stakes
51	increase because athletes are willing to bear additional risk. Demonstrating that game stakes influence injury preva-
52	lence opens new horizons to frame injury policy in term of incentive design, under the general premise that it is possible
53	to influence risk‐taking choices (Cisyk & Courty, 2023a, 2023b).
54	    We investigate whether injury costs depend on game stakes by using the incidence of concussions sustained during
55	National Football League (NFL) regular‐season games. Because concussions have a high potential of lifetime

118	     We find that the swing variable has a statistically significant impact on the incidence of concussions. While the
119	average NFL team faces a 25% chance of observing at least one concussion in a game, this probability increases by 10

121	     We conduct a series of robustness tests. First, we eliminate observations with a large upper bound in the approx-
122	imation error on the swing value. Second, we use the notion of mathematical certainty to improve the swing values. The
123	third robustness approach leverages the sequential feature of the NFL playoff seeding process.2 Finally, we consider
124	different definitions of swing that account for a team's and its opponent's incentives to take risk.
125	     Consistent with Hannah et al. (2019), we do not find any effect of game stakes on the incidence of concussions using
126	mathematical certainly alone, which is a coarse measure of game stakes. In contrast, the swing variable captures finer,
127	team‐specific variation in incentives. We also find results consistent with the literature for confounding variables
128	describing game conditions such as playing surface, team strategy, and weather. These findings contribute to the
129	literature that studies the determinants of concussion in the NFL (e.g., see Heintz et al., 2020 for a recent work). Most
130	importantly, our results have policy implications that we review in the conclusion.
131	     The sports literature has long recognized that athletes respond to game rules, performance incentives, and to the
132	general regulations that govern how to achieve superior performance (Frick, 2003). We argue in Section 2 that the
133	behavioral responses described in the literature do not directly address the risk‐escalation hypothesis, which applies to
134	any sports where risk‐taking increases both the chance from winning and the likelihood of injury. Section 3 introduces
135	our case study of concussion events in the NFL and presents the data. Section 4 explains how we approximate the swing
136	value. Section 5 presents the results and numerous robustness tests. The paper concludes with some implications of our
137	work as well as some limitations.

140	2 | LITERATURE REVIEW AND HYPOTHESIS
141	
142	A large literature has studied numerous determinants of injury in a variety of sports including American football. Part
143	of the literature has looked at factors that are outside the control of athletes. For example, Haider et al. (2018) studies
144	the role of weather while Fair and Champa (2019) looks at game rules. Injuries also happen when an athlete takes
145	excessive risk, by for example, putting strain on the body, selecting strategies that involve body‐contact or falls, or
146	neglecting prevention. There is much evidence that such type of risk increases the chances of exceptional performance
147	at the cost of higher chances of injuries (e.g., Bolling et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2004; Verhagen
148	et al., 2010). Courty and Cisyk (2023a) speculates that athletes can increase their chance of success by taking more risk
149	but suffer higher expected costs of injury. Athletes will assume more risk when the rewards from doing are higher. Our
150	main hypothesis is derived from Lemma 1 in Cisyk and Courty (2023a)3:
151	    Risk‐escalation hypothesis: Injuries increase in likelihood during games with higher stakes.
152	    The risk‐escalation hypothesis is novel in that it directly links injury to game stakes.4 There is much evidence that
153	athletes respond in a variety of ways—including unexpected ones—to changes in game rules, that regulate contact and
154	dangerous play, and to the adoption of safety measures such as mandatory protection equipment (Bradley, 2013;
155	Potter, 2011). Such evidence shows that some injuries are caused by athletes' behavioral responses (Arias et al., 2011;
156	Lybbert et al., 2012; Mack et al., 2021). There is also much evidence that athletes change effort and strategies in response
157	to game stakes (Kahn, 2000). We are not aware, however, of any work that directly connects game stakes and injuries
158	under the premise that athletes increase their risk of injury in response to a game's stakes.
159	    To implement the risk‐escalation hypothesis, one should focus on a type of injury that is caused by risk taking
160	(among other factors), happens frequently, has significant health consequences, and for which the researcher has access
161	to exogenous variation in the incremental gain from taking risk. We choose to focus on concussion because this type of
162	injury has been widely studied and quality data about in‐game injury is available as explained in the next section.5 A
163	common concern with injury data is under‐reporting. Kroshus et al. (2015) suggest that only one in seven concussions

189	3 | CASE STUDY AND DATA
190	
191	3.1 | Case study
192	
193	During our sample period, which covers the 2012 to 2015 seasons, each of the 32 NFL teams play 16 games during the
194	regular season, typically between September and December of each year. At the end of the regular season, 12 of the 32
195	teams qualify to advance to the single‐elimination playoff tournament to determine the season's champions in the finale
196	known as the Super Bowl. Playoff qualification is largely determined on a team's win‐loss record at the end of the season
197	with other considerations accounted for when ties occur (see Supporting Information S1: Appendix 2 for details).
198	    Many regard the playoff games as the pinnacle of American football with Super Bowl viewership regularly reaching
199	over 110 million households from 2012 to 2015. Players are remunerated for participating in playoff games. For the final
200	season of our sample (i.e., 2015) players are compensated a minimum of $23,000 and a maximum of $198,000 for
201	playing in the playoffs (amounts vary by the extent of the team's advancement through the single‐elimination tour-
202	nament). For a player earning the league's minimum salary of $435,000, these bonuses range from five to 45%.8
203	    Concussions are a common injury in American football with devastating life‐changing consequences (Heintz
204	et al., 2020; Navarro et al., 2017). After denying the importance of concussions for years, the NFL has faced multiple
205	lawsuits from injured players (Bull, 2021). To increase player safety, the NFL has begun, staring in the early 2000's, to
206	implement a set of guidelines covering concussion spotters, on‐field medical professionals, film reviews, examination,
207	treatment, and return‐to‐play rules. Supporting Information SI: Appendix 1 provides a list of rule changes implemented
208	during our sample period designed to limit injuries, including concussions. The presence of such rule changes requires
209	the estimation strategy to consider temporal effects, as we discuss in the Identification section below.

215	in regular‐season NFL games, as detailed on official NFL injury reports and collected and summarized by PBS Frontline

217	number of games the player was inactive (if any), and a brief description of the event. The information is summarized

219	juries, the injured body part, the player's level of participation in the weekly practices, and their expected status for the
220	next game (see Data Supporting Information S1: Appendix 1 for details). Only injuries containing the terms
221	“concussion” or “head” are selected.10

253	The swing value measures a team's game stakes as the marginal impact of winning a game on the team's chance to earn
254	a playoff berth.
255	
256	Definition. The swing value of team i for game t is the expected increase in its chance of earning a playoff berth due to
257	winning game t.
258	
259	    This incentive‐based definition differs from past works saying that a game is important if its outcome has a large

263	assert that such a game can still have a large swing value for one (or both) of the teams, as will be the case if the
264	outcome of the game has a large impact on a team's chance to qualify for the playoffs.

1 | INTRODUCTION

Sports injuries are a major concern to athletes, medical experts, and policy makers. Scholars in sports medicine and
sports management have made multiple proposals to minimize the injury cost of participating in sport, such as pre-
vention, treatment, protective equipment mandate, or changes to a sport's rules (Finch, 2006). This existing approach
tends to view injuries as unfortunate yet largely unavoidable accidents.
    In this work, we investigate whether some sports injuries occur because athletes take risk in the pursuit of the
pinnacle of success. According to the risk‐escalation hypothesis, injuries should be more prevalent as competition stakes
increase because athletes are willing to bear additional risk. Demonstrating that game stakes influence injury preva-
lence opens new horizons to frame injury policy in term of incentive design, under the general premise that it is possible
to influence risk‐taking choices (Cisyk & Courty, 2023a, 2023b).
    We investigate whether injury costs depend on game stakes by using the incidence of concussions sustained during
National Football League (NFL) regular‐season games. Because concussions have a high potential of lifetime

exemplified by American football (DeHaven & Lintner, 1986).1 Sports organizations have implemented policies to
increase player safety (Deubert et al., 2017), legislators have passed laws to standardize concussion detection and
diagnosis (Rotolo & Lengefeld, 2020), and players have initiated legal battles that threaten the financial viability of some
professional sports (Bull, 2021).
     Despite being the world's most valuable sports league with massive investments in injury detection, prevention, and
treatment, the NFL still grapples with concussions. Moreover, the NFL offers rigorous reporting of injury events (at least
relative to other sports) subject to strict monitoring and public‐disclosure rules, and a mature literature studying
confounding factors. Finally, the NFL offers an exemplary data laboratory: each of the league's 32 teams play 16 games
during the regular season, some with high stakes, and others not.
     We derive a gauge of game stakes that measures a team's incentive to win a game that we term the game's swing.
The swing represents the increase in the probability that the team qualifies for the post‐season playoffs from winning a
given game. The swing value generalizes the notion of mathematical certainty (i.e., whether a team can still influence
its qualification status) and expands on other measures of game importance used in the literature (Lahvička, 2015; Lei &
Humphreys, 2013; Scarf & Shi, 2008; Schilling, 1994). Computing exact swing values requires considering all possible
future path‐dependent game outcomes, which is beyond computational possibility. Section 4 proposes an approxima-
tion of the swing value and demonstrates that this approximation performs well under two simple and testable con-
ditions that are satisfied for a large fraction of observations in our sample.

and losses (horizontal axis). Although swing values are team‐ and game‐specific, for the sake of the present argument,
it helps looking at averages. As the season progresses, fewer games remain, and teams move further away from the

if the team has won five and lost four, it faces a swing value of 24, saying that it increases its chance of qualifying for the
playoffs by 24 percentage points by collecting its sixth win in its 10th game. In contrast, the swing values are at most 3
percentage points if the team has already won at least eight games or lost at least six: the playoff outcomes are nearly
forgone conclusions regardless of future performance.
     We find that the swing variable has a statistically significant impact on the incidence of concussions. While the
average NFL team faces a 25% chance of observing at least one concussion in a game, this probability increases by 10
percentage points when a win increases one of the teams' odds of playoff contention by 40 percentage points.
     We conduct a series of robustness tests. First, we eliminate observations with a large upper bound in the approx-
imation error on the swing value. Second, we use the notion of mathematical certainty to improve the swing values. The
third robustness approach leverages the sequential feature of the NFL playoff seeding process.2 Finally, we consider
different definitions of swing that account for a team's and its opponent's incentives to take risk.
     Consistent with Hannah et al. (2019), we do not find any effect of game stakes on the incidence of concussions using
mathematical certainly alone, which is a coarse measure of game stakes. In contrast, the swing variable captures finer,
team‐specific variation in incentives. We also find results consistent with the literature for confounding variables
describing game conditions such as playing surface, team strategy, and weather. These findings contribute to the
literature that studies the determinants of concussion in the NFL (e.g., see Heintz et al., 2020 for a recent work). Most
importantly, our results have policy implications that we review in the conclusion.
     The sports literature has long recognized that athletes respond to game rules, performance incentives, and to the
general regulations that govern how to achieve superior performance (Frick, 2003). We argue in Section 2 that the
behavioral responses described in the literature do not directly address the risk‐escalation hypothesis, which applies to
any sports where risk‐taking increases both the chance from winning and the likelihood of injury. Section 3 introduces
our case study of concussion events in the NFL and presents the data. Section 4 explains how we approximate the swing
value. Section 5 presents the results and numerous robustness tests. The paper concludes with some implications of our
work as well as some limitations.


2 | LITERATURE REVIEW AND HYPOTHESIS

A large literature has studied numerous determinants of injury in a variety of sports including American football. Part
of the literature has looked at factors that are outside the control of athletes. For example, Haider et al. (2018) studies
the role of weather while Fair and Champa (2019) looks at game rules. Injuries also happen when an athlete takes
excessive risk, by for example, putting strain on the body, selecting strategies that involve body‐contact or falls, or
neglecting prevention. There is much evidence that such type of risk increases the chances of exceptional performance
at the cost of higher chances of injuries (e.g., Bolling et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2004; Verhagen
et al., 2010). Courty and Cisyk (2023a) speculates that athletes can increase their chance of success by taking more risk
but suffer higher expected costs of injury. Athletes will assume more risk when the rewards from doing are higher. Our
main hypothesis is derived from Lemma 1 in Cisyk and Courty (2023a)3:
    Risk‐escalation hypothesis: Injuries increase in likelihood during games with higher stakes.
    The risk‐escalation hypothesis is novel in that it directly links injury to game stakes.4 There is much evidence that
athletes respond in a variety of ways—including unexpected ones—to changes in game rules, that regulate contact and
dangerous play, and to the adoption of safety measures such as mandatory protection equipment (Bradley, 2013;
Potter, 2011). Such evidence shows that some injuries are caused by athletes' behavioral responses (Arias et al., 2011;
Lybbert et al., 2012; Mack et al., 2021). There is also much evidence that athletes change effort and strategies in response
to game stakes (Kahn, 2000). We are not aware, however, of any work that directly connects game stakes and injuries
under the premise that athletes increase their risk of injury in response to a game's stakes.
    To implement the risk‐escalation hypothesis, one should focus on a type of injury that is caused by risk taking
(among other factors), happens frequently, has significant health consequences, and for which the researcher has access
to exogenous variation in the incremental gain from taking risk. We choose to focus on concussion because this type of
injury has been widely studied and quality data about in‐game injury is available as explained in the next section.5 A
common concern with injury data is under‐reporting. Kroshus et al. (2015) suggest that only one in seven concussions

3 | CASE STUDY AND DATA

3.1 | Case study

During our sample period, which covers the 2012 to 2015 seasons, each of the 32 NFL teams play 16 games during the
regular season, typically between September and December of each year. At the end of the regular season, 12 of the 32
teams qualify to advance to the single‐elimination playoff tournament to determine the season's champions in the finale
known as the Super Bowl. Playoff qualification is largely determined on a team's win‐loss record at the end of the season
with other considerations accounted for when ties occur (see Supporting Information S1: Appendix 2 for details).
    Many regard the playoff games as the pinnacle of American football with Super Bowl viewership regularly reaching
over 110 million households from 2012 to 2015. Players are remunerated for participating in playoff games. For the final
season of our sample (i.e., 2015) players are compensated a minimum of $23,000 and a maximum of $198,000 for
playing in the playoffs (amounts vary by the extent of the team's advancement through the single‐elimination tour-
nament). For a player earning the league's minimum salary of $435,000, these bonuses range from five to 45%.8
    Concussions are a common injury in American football with devastating life‐changing consequences (Heintz
et al., 2020; Navarro et al., 2017). After denying the importance of concussions for years, the NFL has faced multiple
lawsuits from injured players (Bull, 2021). To increase player safety, the NFL has begun, staring in the early 2000's, to
implement a set of guidelines covering concussion spotters, on‐field medical professionals, film reviews, examination,
treatment, and return‐to‐play rules. Supporting Information SI: Appendix 1 provides a list of rule changes implemented
during our sample period designed to limit injuries, including concussions. The presence of such rule changes requires
the estimation strategy to consider temporal effects, as we discuss in the Identification section below.


3.2 | Data

We combine data from numerous publicly available sources. Our variable of interest is the concussion events sustained
in regular‐season NFL games, as detailed on official NFL injury reports and collected and summarized by PBS Frontline
Concussion Watch.9 The data contain information on the individual, position, team, the date of the concussion, the
number of games the player was inactive (if any), and a brief description of the event. The information is summarized
from official weekly injury reports released by each NFL team. These reports list all players that have reportable in-
juries, the injured body part, the player's level of participation in the weekly practices, and their expected status for the
next game (see Data Supporting Information S1: Appendix 1 for details). Only injuries containing the terms
“concussion” or “head” are selected.10

4 | SWING VALUES AND IDENTIFICATION

The swing value measures a team's game stakes as the marginal impact of winning a game on the team's chance to earn
a playoff berth.

Definition. The swing value of team i for game t is the expected increase in its chance of earning a playoff berth due to
winning game t.

impact on end‐of‐season‐outcomes (Geenens, 2014; Schilling, 1994). For example, Lahvička (2015) defines importance
as the “strength of relationship between the match result and a given season outcome.” According to Lahvička, a game
that features a strong team against a weak one is unimportant because the outcome is almost certain. In contrast, we
assert that such a game can still have a large swing value for one (or both) of the teams, as will be the case if the
outcome of the game has a large impact on a team's chance to qualify for the playoffs.

4.1 | Payoff function, conditions 1 and 2, and swing values

The shape of the payoff function is important for several reasons. First, a payoff function that closely resembles a step
function, even though not exactly, will likely deliver good approximation of the swing values (because conditions 1 and
2 are more likely to hold). Second, the shape of the payoff function also influences whether the swing value varies.
Specifically, the swing values are constant when the payoff function is a linear function of W: teams face the same
incentives throughout the season, and it is not possible to identify the effect of swing value on injuries.

that the payoff function is weakly increasing in Wi,T. A team that has won seven or fewer games at the end of the season
has effectively zero chance to qualify for the playoffs (A(W) = 0) while a team that has won 11 games or more is certain
to do so (A(W) = 1). Since the payoff probability increases approximately between seven and 11 wins, the incentive zone
is Z = {7,8,9,10}. The non‐linearity in the payoff function implies that the reward from winning one additional game is
not constant: a team has a strong incentive to win one more game if it otherwise expects to win 10 games by the end of

840	6 | CONCLUSION
841	
842	We show that the incidence of concussions sustained during NFL regular‐season games depend on the benefit that the
843	competing teams receive from winning a game in terms of the incremental chance from qualifying for the playoff. A
844	team's chance to suffers at least one concussion increases by 10 percentage points in a game where a win increases one
845	of the team's odds of playoff selection by 40 percentage points. This is the first evidence in support of the risk‐escalation
846	hypothesis stating that injuries increase with competition stakes. This establishes a starting point to assess the role of
847	risk‐taking incentives on athletes' injuries. For example, one may conjecture that our measured impact of game stakes
848	on concussions applies to other injuries beyond concussions, and to other sports beyond professional American football.

    Random variations in game outcomes generate variations in the incentives to take risk, or to face a team that is
likely to take risk, and this establishes the foundation for our identification strategy. Still, one must consider other
mechanisms that could generate an association between the swing variable and injury. Team strategy could influence
both injury and the likelihood that a team stays within playoff contention late within a season. For example, consider a
team that employs a strategy that has a high chance of injury in addition to a high variance of success (the team can do
extremely well and win most games or extremely poorly and lose most). This generates an opposite prediction to ours.
The teams that select this strategy have low swing values and high injury rates relative to the other teams (high swing
values and low injury rates). Team fixed effects control for unobserved team characteristics, including team strategies.
    Beyond this, it is not clear why injury outcomes should be associated with swing values. Clearly, injury outcomes
lower future expected performance if they constrain the set of players that can be fielded, but the impact on swing is
ambiguous.15 Although we cannot control for unobserved changes in team strategies that could influence both injury
rates and swing values, we investigate the issue empirically in Supporting Information S1: Appendix A5. We find no
relation between past injury outcomes on future swing values. This suggests that there is no causal link from injuries
toward swing.

We first discuss the results of estimating Equation (3). Then, we check whether the predictions of the control variables
are aligned with the literature, and most importantly, we compare the magnitude of the swing coefficient with the
magnitude of the control variables that have received attention in earlier works. Finally, we demonstrate that the main
conclusion survive a barrage of robustness checks.

team needs to travel increases the probability of a concussion by roughly 0.7 percentage points. For example, the ex-
pected incidence of a concussion for the Pittsburgh Steelers would be 0.7 percentage points higher if it were to play the
Dallas Cowboys (932 miles of travel required) than the Tennessee Titans (471 miles). Among other controls considered,
the use of an artificial playing surface, instead of grass, increases the risk of concussion by 6–7 percentage points. Despite
the dangers of artificial turf being well‐known—particularly for soft‐tissue joint injuries—and despite complaints from
NFL players and their union (Tretter, 2020), 44% of the games within our sample were played on artificial turf. The team
strategy variables are largely insignificant with the exception of playing against a team that uses the “Air Coryell” offense
strategy, which lowers the incidence of concussion by about 9 percentage points. Others (e.g., Teramoto et al., 2015) have
found a significant impact of style of play characterized by a hastened pace of game play often requiring offensive players
to catch the football at a time where their bodies are in positions vulnerable to unforeseen contact (i.e., “slant” routes).
    Since NFL games are played in a combination of indoor and outdoor venues, we study how weather conditions
impact injuries. Consistent with Haider et al. (2018), we find that the probability of a concussion decreases with higher
temperatures and in worse weather conditions. Moderate snow has a large impact on the incidence of a concussion
(decreases in concussion rates of 23–31 percentage points). Heavy rain and moderate rain also decrease the chance of
concussion but this result is statistically significant only when game fixed effects are not included. These results must be
interpreted with care because two competing effects may influence the impact of weather on injury: first, weather can
directly affect the risk of injury (e.g., precipitation causes sleek playing surfaces). Second, and in contrast to the first,
contest theory suggests that inclement weather adds noise in the determination of the outcome, thereby lowering the
incentive to invest in risky strategies. According to Lazear and Rosen (1981), contestants invest less effort when luck
plays a larger role in selecting the winner. We are unable to separate the direct playing‐condition effect from the in-
direct behavioral response to the increase in luck.17
    Overall, the impact on concussions is small for most control variables compared to the swing variable. Although
weather conditions may have a large impact, this could be due to a decreased incentive effect. This suggests that in-
centives play a large role in explaining concussions, especially for high‐swing games that take place at the end of the
season, relative to other determinants of concussion that have received much attention in the literature. For example, a
game in which a win guarantees a team a playoff berth (i.e., a swing value of one) increases the probability of a
concussion by roughly four times as much as the impact of playing on an artificial surface.

We show that the incidence of concussions sustained during NFL regular‐season games depend on the benefit that the
competing teams receive from winning a game in terms of the incremental chance from qualifying for the playoff. A
team's chance to suffers at least one concussion increases by 10 percentage points in a game where a win increases one
of the team's odds of playoff selection by 40 percentage points. This is the first evidence in support of the risk‐escalation
hypothesis stating that injuries increase with competition stakes. This establishes a starting point to assess the role of
risk‐taking incentives on athletes' injuries. For example, one may conjecture that our measured impact of game stakes
on concussions applies to other injuries beyond concussions, and to other sports beyond professional American football.

861	Sports and health professionals have searched for causal factors that explain injuries and that have actionable impli-
862	cations. According to the contingency view, injuries are the consequence of controllable external conditions (e.g.,
863	weather, surface, game rules).19 However, many doubt that the margin of improvement from the contingency view will

867	premise that it is possible to prevent some sport injuries by incentivizing behavior. In return, one can draw lessons to

A methodological contribution of our study is to construct an incentive‐based measure, which we call the swing, of
the importance of a game for a team and to propose a computationally friendly method to approximate it. The swing
measure varies across teams and games of a season because of (a) heterogeneity in team quality; (b) luck (i.e., game
outcomes are uncertain); and, most importantly, (c) the non‐linear nature of playoff contention. The results demon-
strate the importance of accounting for unobserved team heterogeneity (e.g., strength, strategy, etc.), while at the same
time accounting for how team quality modulates how the swing variable responds to past outcomes.
    Although this paper studies concussions, the methodology can be deployed to answer other questions. One could, of
course, study the prevalence of other injuries but, more generally, one could construct swing variables in other sports
having a similar two‐stage competition structure as American football (e.g., Champions League qualification in Eu-
ropean soccer), while investigating other behavior (e.g., by players, teams, fans, advertisers, etc.) that should respond to
changes in game stakes.
    The risk‐escalation hypothesis also offers a strong motivation to seriously consider the health cost of incentives.
Sports and health professionals have searched for causal factors that explain injuries and that have actionable impli-
cations. According to the contingency view, injuries are the consequence of controllable external conditions (e.g.,
weather, surface, game rules).19 However, many doubt that the margin of improvement from the contingency view will
be sufficient to appease the critics who, for example, oppose youth participation in dangerous sports, or question the
long‐term viability of sports that have high life‐altering injury rates (Bull, 2021).
    Our evidence in support of the risk‐escalation hypothesis offers a new way to think about injury policy, based on the
premise that it is possible to prevent some sport injuries by incentivizing behavior. In return, one can draw lessons to
inform policy and practice, best summarized in the context of American football as following: Coaches, administrators,
and players should be made aware that, although most concussions are unfortunate and random accidents, they are also
sometimes caused by controllable determinants. Long travel time by visiting team and artificial playing surfaces tend to
increase the likelihood of concussion, and, as our research shows, concussions happen more frequently in high stake
games, and in particular those game that determine whether a team is likely to qualify for the playoffs. Teams and
players should carefully assess the injury cost of exerting maximal effort in these games. Organizers, such as the Na-
tional Football League, should take heed that compliance and enforcement of in‐game concussion detection should
depend on a game's stakes (e.g., have more concussion spotters in high‐swing games) and should regulate athlete
incentives to de‐escalate risk taking (e.g., long return‐to‐play rules and caps on financial bonuses in high‐swing
competitions).

15	Abstract
16	In this review, we examine the literature in light of the mechanical principles that govern linear accelerated running. While the
17	scientific literature concerning sprint mechanics is comprehensive, these principles of fundamental mechanics present some
18	pitfalls which can (and does) lead to misinterpretations of findings. Various models of sprint mechanics, most of which build
19	on the spring–mass paradigm, are discussed with reference to both the insight they provide and their limitations. Although
20	much research confirms that sprinters to some extent behave like a spring–mass system with regard to gross kinematics (step
21	length, step rate, ground contact time, and lower limb deformation), the laws of motion, supported by empirical evidence,
22	show that applying the spring–mass model for accelerated running has flaws. It is essential to appreciate that models are pre-
23	set interpretations of reality; finding that a model describes the motor behaviour well is not proof of the mechanism behind
24	the model. Recent efforts to relate sprinting mechanics to metabolic demands are promising, but have the same limitation of
25	being model based. Furthermore, a large proportion of recent literature focuses on the interaction between total and horizontal
26	(end-goal) force. We argue that this approach has limitations concerning fundamental sprinting mechanics. Moreover, power
27	analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed. In closing, some prominent practical concepts and didactics in sprint
28	running are discussed in light of the mechanical principles presented. Ultimately, whereas the basic principles of sprinting
29	are relatively simple, the way an athlete manages the mechanical constraints and opportunities is far more complex.

    INVITED REVIEW



Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice—a review
Thomas Haugen1           · David McGhie2 · Gertjan Ettema2

Received: 8 February 2019 / Accepted: 4 April 2019
© Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2019


Abstract
In this review, we examine the literature in light of the mechanical principles that govern linear accelerated running. While the
scientific literature concerning sprint mechanics is comprehensive, these principles of fundamental mechanics present some
pitfalls which can (and does) lead to misinterpretations of findings. Various models of sprint mechanics, most of which build
on the spring–mass paradigm, are discussed with reference to both the insight they provide and their limitations. Although
much research confirms that sprinters to some extent behave like a spring–mass system with regard to gross kinematics (step
length, step rate, ground contact time, and lower limb deformation), the laws of motion, supported by empirical evidence,
show that applying the spring–mass model for accelerated running has flaws. It is essential to appreciate that models are pre-
set interpretations of reality; finding that a model describes the motor behaviour well is not proof of the mechanism behind
the model. Recent efforts to relate sprinting mechanics to metabolic demands are promising, but have the same limitation of
being model based. Furthermore, a large proportion of recent literature focuses on the interaction between total and horizontal
(end-goal) force. We argue that this approach has limitations concerning fundamental sprinting mechanics. Moreover, power
analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed. In closing, some prominent practical concepts and didactics in sprint
running are discussed in light of the mechanical principles presented. Ultimately, whereas the basic principles of sprinting
are relatively simple, the way an athlete manages the mechanical constraints and opportunities is far more complex.

Keywords Running technique · Kinetics · Stiffness · Braking · Propulsion · Power

76	                                           Introduction
77	                                           Performing soccer-specific actions at high speed is a paramount physical feature of high-level
78	                                           soccer players. Short accelerations and linear sprints are two of the most important actions in
79	                                           soccer since they frequently precede goals and other decisive actions [1]. On the other hand,
80	                                           the majority of hamstring injuries (57%) occur during high-speed sprinting actions [2]. Specif-
81	                                           ically, hamstring muscle injuries (HMI) are the most prevalent injuries in soccer accounting
82	                                           for 12–16% of all injuries [3] and have not shown signs of clear decrease over the last three
83	                                           decades. Therefore, it seems logical to expect sprinting to be a key parameter in soccer both
84	                                           from a performance and injury point of view. Both the swing and the stance phase of sprinting,
85	                                           where the hamstring muscles are put under tension while lengthening (eccentric musculoten-
86	                                           dinous contraction) to decelerate knee extension have been suggested as possible scenarios of
87	                                           injury occurrence [4,5] and have laid the foundations of current prevention methods (eccen-
88	                                           tric strength training) of HMI in soccer [6].
89	                                               Research suggests that this type of eccentric training results in a multifactorial adaptative
90	                                           response possibly including increases in motor unit discharge rate and changes in muscle
91	                                           architecture such as hypertrophy and fascicle lengthening [7–9]. Specifically, repeated expo-
92	                                           sure to lengthening hamstring contractions through the nordic hamstring exercise (NHE)
93	                                           seems to protect muscles from injury in soccer [6]. The main mechanism proposed by the
94	                                           authors is the increase in fascicle length, supposedly induced by an increase in the number of
95	                                           sarcomeres in series, which in turn results in less overall strain and also lower susceptibility to
96	                                           damage [10]. Moreover, Timmins et al. [8] have recently observed such an adaptation after
97	                                           eccentric knee flexor training on an isokinetic dynamometer while also noting that concentric
98	                                           training caused fascicle shortening, despite occurring at long muscle lengths. Furthermore, the
99	                                           same group of authors recently reported that soccer players with shorter biceps femoris long
100	                                           head (BFlh) fascicles (<10.56 cm on average) were at fourfold greater risk of hamstring strain
101	                                           injury than players with longer fascicles [11]. It is however important to keep in mind that
102	                                           clear methodological limitations are associated with ultrasound methodology to infer muscle
103	                                           fascicle lengths [12,13] as will be discussed below. Given the effectiveness of the predominantly
104	                                           eccentric NHE in increasing eccentric hamstring strength when added to soccer training [14],
105	                                           it is important to examine the impact of this single exercise on BFlh fascicle lengths concomi-
106	                                           tantly to real soccer practice and not only in isolated conditions.
107	                                               In addition to its potential role in preventing posterior thigh muscle strains, hamstring
108	                                           muscle strength has been suggested as an important factor to improve sprinting performance
109	                                           in soccer as a horizontal force producer [15,16]. During the acceleration phase of sprinting,
110	                                           forward orientation of ground reaction force (GRF) has been shown to be the most powerful
111	                                           determinant of field sprint performance compared to the overall magnitude of vertical or
112	                                           resultant GRF [17]. Recently, Morin et al. [17] have shown that hamstring EMG activity during
113	                                           the swing phase and eccentric knee flexor peak torque were related to the amount of horizontal

122	                                           GRF produced during treadmill sprint accelerations converting the hamstrings as a key mus-
123	                                           cular determinant of sprint acceleration performance. These results suggest that the conjunc-
124	                                           tion of hip extensors (hamstrings in particular) torque capability and degree of activation
125	                                           during the swing phase, is a key muscular determinant of sprint acceleration performance
126	                                           [17]. This important role of the posterior thigh muscles during sprinting could partly explain
127	                                           the altered capability to produce horizontal force at low speed during the first meters of the
128	                                           acceleration phase shown by soccer players after return to sport from a hamstring injury [18].
129	                                               Different types of hamstring-focused strength training have been proposed in the literature
130	                                           to improve sprint performance in soccer players [14,16] but the direct, individual relationship
131	                                           between improvements in single joint hamstring strength and sprint performance and
132	                                           mechanics remains unclear. Interestingly, to date, no study exists about the effect of sprint
133	                                           practice (recently suggested as a potentially preventive method in adequate doses) [19,20], as a
134	                                           complementary training on the muscle architecture of soccer players. The velocity at which an
135	                                           athlete runs once at full speed or close is directly related to the velocity of the lower limb seg-
136	                                           ments during the swing phase, and in turn the negative work done by the hamstrings [3] since
137	                                           they are significant contributors to human propulsion at very high speeds [17,21]. Further-
138	                                           more, in addition to the significant length-tension sustained by the hamstring muscle-tendon
139	                                           unit during maximal velocity running [22], this specific exercise is the only one, by far, that
140	                                           elicits maximal levels of hamstring activity as assessed by surface electromyography [23,24]. It
141	                                           is expected that a comprehensive sprint training program may induce an overall improvement
142	                                           of sprint performance and underlying mechanical outputs, and BFlh structural adaptations
143	                                           associated to this eccentric-type overload for the muscle-tendon unit, including a greater fasci-
144	                                           cle length. Given the time constraint of modern soccer training, specific NHE or sprint train-
145	                                           ing might not be systematically implemented [25], raising the question of their respective
146	                                           effectiveness as complementary interventions to the soccer training content.
147	                                               The aim of this study was to compare the effects of hamstring eccentric (NHE) strength
148	                                           training versus sprint training programmed as complements to regular soccer practice, on
149	                                           sprint performance and its mechanical underpinnings, and BFlh architecture.

151	                                           Materials and methods
152	                                           Procedure
153	                                           In this prospective interventional controlled study, sprint performance, mechanics and BFlh
154	                                           architecture variables were measured before and after six weeks of training during the first six
155	                                           preseason weeks in three different groups of soccer players. The “Soccer group” (controls) con-
156	                                           tinuing their usual soccer practice, the “Nordic group” players performed a NHE program in
157	                                           addition to usual soccer practice, and the “Sprint group” performed a comprehensive sprint
158	                                           acceleration program in addition to usual soccer practice. All subjects were informed of poten-
159	                                           tial risks associated with the experimental procedures before giving their written informed
160	                                           consent to participate and ethics approval was granted by the Faculty of Sports of the Univer-
161	                                           sity of Porto, Portugal human research ethics committee, which conforms to the ethical stan-
162	                                           dards established by the declaration of Helsinki.

166	                                           sion of Football Association of Porto, North of Portugal. Within each team, players were ran-
167	                                           domly assigned to the different groups for the study. The possible effect of the training load on
168	                                           the study outcomes were mitigated by having all players proportionally distributed, and both
169	                                           teams following very close training and game programs and physical demands. Soccer teams

196	                                           Sprint performance and mechanics measurements
197	                                           After a standardized warm-up, subjects performed two 50 m maximal sprints, separated by 6
198	                                           min of passive rest, from a standing start on an artificial turf field with their habitual soccer
199	                                           boots. Tests were performed by the same investigator (FC), at the same time of the day (always
200	                                           before of their normal soccer training), under similar environmental conditions of tempera-
201	                                           ture. Each sprint was measured by means of a Radar device with a 46.9 Hz sampling frequency
202	                                           (Stalker ATS II Version 5.0.2.1, Applied Concepts, Dallas, TX, USA), which was placed on a
203	                                           tripod 10 meters behind the subjects at a height of 1 meter corresponding approximately to the
204	                                           height of subjects’ center of mass [26,27]. From these speed–time measurements, a macro-
205	                                           scopic biomechanical analysis-based on the laws of motion [28] was used to calculate the maxi-
206	                                           mal horizontal external power (Pmax (W�kg-1)), velocity (v0 (m�s-1)) and force (F0 (N�kg-1))
207	                                           mechanical outputs during the acceleration. In addition, the ratio of force was calculated as the
208	                                           horizontal component of the ground reaction force divided by the resultant ground reaction
209	                                           force, and the maximal value of this ratio (RFmax (%)) was used as an indicator of the players
210	                                           ability to orient the ground reaction force in the forward direction at the beginning of their
211	                                           acceleration. The higher the RFmax, the more forward the force orientation during the early
212	                                           phase of acceleration. Finally, sprint performance was described via the measurement of 5 m
213	                                           (s) and 20 m (s) times, as derived from the fitted speed-time curves (see [28] for more details)
214	                                           [28].

222	                                           The measurement site was the halfway point between the ischial tuberosity and the posterior
223	                                           knee joint fold, along the line of the BFlh. Once the scanning site was determined in each par-
224	                                           ticipant, several anatomical landmarks were taken (ischial tuberosity, fibula head and mid-
225	                                           point of the posterior knee joint fold) and photographs were taken in order to ensure

                                           Introduction
                                           Performing soccer-specific actions at high speed is a paramount physical feature of high-level

                                           soccer since they frequently precede goals and other decisive actions [1]. On the other hand,
                                           the majority of hamstring injuries (57%) occur during high-speed sprinting actions [2]. Specif-
                                           ically, hamstring muscle injuries (HMI) are the most prevalent injuries in soccer accounting
                                           for 12–16% of all injuries [3] and have not shown signs of clear decrease over the last three
                                           decades. Therefore, it seems logical to expect sprinting to be a key parameter in soccer both
                                           from a performance and injury point of view. Both the swing and the stance phase of sprinting,
                                           where the hamstring muscles are put under tension while lengthening (eccentric musculoten-
                                           dinous contraction) to decelerate knee extension have been suggested as possible scenarios of
                                           injury occurrence [4,5] and have laid the foundations of current prevention methods (eccen-
                                           tric strength training) of HMI in soccer [6].
                                               Research suggests that this type of eccentric training results in a multifactorial adaptative
                                           response possibly including increases in motor unit discharge rate and changes in muscle
                                           architecture such as hypertrophy and fascicle lengthening [7–9]. Specifically, repeated expo-
                                           sure to lengthening hamstring contractions through the nordic hamstring exercise (NHE)
                                           seems to protect muscles from injury in soccer [6]. The main mechanism proposed by the
                                           authors is the increase in fascicle length, supposedly induced by an increase in the number of
                                           sarcomeres in series, which in turn results in less overall strain and also lower susceptibility to
                                           damage [10]. Moreover, Timmins et al. [8] have recently observed such an adaptation after
                                           eccentric knee flexor training on an isokinetic dynamometer while also noting that concentric
                                           training caused fascicle shortening, despite occurring at long muscle lengths. Furthermore, the
                                           same group of authors recently reported that soccer players with shorter biceps femoris long
                                           head (BFlh) fascicles (<10.56 cm on average) were at fourfold greater risk of hamstring strain
                                           injury than players with longer fascicles [11]. It is however important to keep in mind that
                                           clear methodological limitations are associated with ultrasound methodology to infer muscle
                                           fascicle lengths [12,13] as will be discussed below. Given the effectiveness of the predominantly
                                           eccentric NHE in increasing eccentric hamstring strength when added to soccer training [14],
                                           it is important to examine the impact of this single exercise on BFlh fascicle lengths concomi-
                                           tantly to real soccer practice and not only in isolated conditions.
                                               In addition to its potential role in preventing posterior thigh muscle strains, hamstring
                                           muscle strength has been suggested as an important factor to improve sprinting performance
                                           in soccer as a horizontal force producer [15,16]. During the acceleration phase of sprinting,
                                           forward orientation of ground reaction force (GRF) has been shown to be the most powerful
                                           determinant of field sprint performance compared to the overall magnitude of vertical or
                                           resultant GRF [17]. Recently, Morin et al. [17] have shown that hamstring EMG activity during
                                           the swing phase and eccentric knee flexor peak torque were related to the amount of horizontal



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0228283 February 11, 2020                                                                      2 / 19
                                                                                  Architectural and performance effects of different training programs



                                           GRF produced during treadmill sprint accelerations converting the hamstrings as a key mus-
                                           cular determinant of sprint acceleration performance. These results suggest that the conjunc-
                                           tion of hip extensors (hamstrings in particular) torque capability and degree of activation
                                           during the swing phase, is a key muscular determinant of sprint acceleration performance
                                           [17]. This important role of the posterior thigh muscles during sprinting could partly explain
                                           the altered capability to produce horizontal force at low speed during the first meters of the
                                           acceleration phase shown by soccer players after return to sport from a hamstring injury [18].
                                               Different types of hamstring-focused strength training have been proposed in the literature
                                           to improve sprint performance in soccer players [14,16] but the direct, individual relationship
                                           between improvements in single joint hamstring strength and sprint performance and
                                           mechanics remains unclear. Interestingly, to date, no study exists about the effect of sprint
                                           practice (recently suggested as a potentially preventive method in adequate doses) [19,20], as a
                                           complementary training on the muscle architecture of soccer players. The velocity at which an
                                           athlete runs once at full speed or close is directly related to the velocity of the lower limb seg-
                                           ments during the swing phase, and in turn the negative work done by the hamstrings [3] since
                                           they are significant contributors to human propulsion at very high speeds [17,21]. Further-
                                           more, in addition to the significant length-tension sustained by the hamstring muscle-tendon
                                           unit during maximal velocity running [22], this specific exercise is the only one, by far, that
                                           elicits maximal levels of hamstring activity as assessed by surface electromyography [23,24]. It
                                           is expected that a comprehensive sprint training program may induce an overall improvement
                                           of sprint performance and underlying mechanical outputs, and BFlh structural adaptations
                                           associated to this eccentric-type overload for the muscle-tendon unit, including a greater fasci-
                                           cle length. Given the time constraint of modern soccer training, specific NHE or sprint train-
                                           ing might not be systematically implemented [25], raising the question of their respective
                                           effectiveness as complementary interventions to the soccer training content.
                                               The aim of this study was to compare the effects of hamstring eccentric (NHE) strength
                                           training versus sprint training programmed as complements to regular soccer practice, on
                                           sprint performance and its mechanical underpinnings, and BFlh architecture.

                                           Materials and methods
                                           Procedure
                                           In this prospective interventional controlled study, sprint performance, mechanics and BFlh
                                           architecture variables were measured before and after six weeks of training during the first six
                                           preseason weeks in three different groups of soccer players. The “Soccer group” (controls) con-
                                           tinuing their usual soccer practice, the “Nordic group” players performed a NHE program in
                                           addition to usual soccer practice, and the “Sprint group” performed a comprehensive sprint
                                           acceleration program in addition to usual soccer practice. All subjects were informed of poten-
                                           tial risks associated with the experimental procedures before giving their written informed
                                           consent to participate and ethics approval was granted by the Faculty of Sports of the Univer-
                                           sity of Porto, Portugal human research ethics committee, which conforms to the ethical stan-
                                           dards established by the declaration of Helsinki.

                                           Participants
                                           Soccer players were recruited from two different soccer teams playing in the same Elite Divi-
                                           sion of Football Association of Porto, North of Portugal. Within each team, players were ran-
                                           domly assigned to the different groups for the study. The possible effect of the training load on
                                           the study outcomes were mitigated by having all players proportionally distributed, and both
                                           teams following very close training and game programs and physical demands. Soccer teams
