                                                                                 Architectural and performance effects of different training programs



                                           were initially contacted and informed about the project via email. Inclusion criteria were: 1) to
                                           be older than 18 years; 2) to have a competitive experience in soccer for at least 3 consecutive
                                           years prior to measurements; and 3) to start the preseason at the scheduled time. Exclusion cri-
                                           teria were: 1) to be involved in any additional strength training program; 2) to present a history
                                           of hip, knee, or lumbo-pelvic joints injury in the past three years confirmed by MRI and that
                                           required intervention by a health professional, and 3) to suffer a neurological, cardiorespira-
                                           tory or systemic disorder. 32 soccer players (16±6 per team) were voluntarily recruited and
                                           randomly assigned to either “Soccer group” (n = 10), “Nordic group” (n = 12), or “Sprint
                                           group” (n = 10). To reduce potential confounding, a match-pair design was used in which ath-
                                           letes were matched depending on their position (i.e., defender, midfield, and forward), playing
                                           status (i.e., starting or substitute player), and previous hamstring injury.
                                               Nine players dropped out from the study: two from the “Soccer group” due to retirement
                                           form soccer and change to another club; five from the “Nordic group” due to a compliance of
                                           <80% to the training program (n = 3), one semitendinosus injury and one ankle injury; and
                                           two from the “Sprint group” due to both knee injury and adductor longus tear. All players
                                           trained four times per week during 90 minutes and played at least 180 minutes of friendly
                                           matches during the preseason period.

                                           Sprint performance and mechanics measurements
                                           After a standardized warm-up, subjects performed two 50 m maximal sprints, separated by 6
                                           min of passive rest, from a standing start on an artificial turf field with their habitual soccer
                                           boots. Tests were performed by the same investigator (FC), at the same time of the day (always
                                           before of their normal soccer training), under similar environmental conditions of tempera-
                                           ture. Each sprint was measured by means of a Radar device with a 46.9 Hz sampling frequency
                                           (Stalker ATS II Version 5.0.2.1, Applied Concepts, Dallas, TX, USA), which was placed on a
                                           tripod 10 meters behind the subjects at a height of 1 meter corresponding approximately to the
                                           height of subjects’ center of mass [26,27]. From these speed–time measurements, a macro-
                                           scopic biomechanical analysis-based on the laws of motion [28] was used to calculate the maxi-
                                           mal horizontal external power (Pmax (W�kg-1)), velocity (v0 (m�s-1)) and force (F0 (N�kg-1))
                                           mechanical outputs during the acceleration. In addition, the ratio of force was calculated as the
                                           horizontal component of the ground reaction force divided by the resultant ground reaction
                                           force, and the maximal value of this ratio (RFmax (%)) was used as an indicator of the players
                                           ability to orient the ground reaction force in the forward direction at the beginning of their
                                           acceleration. The higher the RFmax, the more forward the force orientation during the early
                                           phase of acceleration. Finally, sprint performance was described via the measurement of 5 m
                                           (s) and 20 m (s) times, as derived from the fitted speed-time curves (see [28] for more details)
                                           [28].

                                           Assessment of the BFlh architecture
                                           BFlh muscle architectural characteristics has been performed using ultrasound following pre-
                                           viously published procedure [29,30]. Muscle thickness (Thickness BFlh), pennation angle (PA)
                                           and the estimation of fascile length (FL) were determined from ultrasound images obtained
                                           along the longitudinal axis of the muscle belly using a 2D B-mode ultrasound (12 Mhz fre-
                                           quency, 8 cm depth; 14 x 47 mm field of view) (GE Healthcare Logiq S7, Wauwatosa, USA).
                                           The measurement site was the halfway point between the ischial tuberosity and the posterior
                                           knee joint fold, along the line of the BFlh. Once the scanning site was determined in each par-
                                           ticipant, several anatomical landmarks were taken (ischial tuberosity, fibula head and mid-
                                           point of the posterior knee joint fold) and photographs were taken in order to ensure



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0228283 February 11, 2020                                                                     4 / 19
                                                                                  Architectural and performance effects of different training programs



                                           reproducibility for future assessment sessions. All architectural measurements were performed
                                           after at least 5 minutes of inactivity, with the participant in prone position, with the hip in neu-
                                           tral position, and the knee positioned passively in full extension with their feet laying off the
                                           bed for comfort and they were instructed to remain relaxed during image acquisition. To
                                           obtain the images, the transducer was then aligned to the fascicle plane, which was assumed to
                                           correspond to the image with the most continuous and visible muscle fascicles (~25% or more
                                           of the total estimated length as a minimum) while the superficial and intermediate aponeuro-
                                           ses remained parallel (less than 4º between aponeuroses angle) in order to meet the stablished
                                           inclusion criteria [30]. For all scans, the probe was handled carefully by the sonographer (MF)
                                           and transmission gel was used to improve the acoustic contact and to keep the transducer pres-
                                           sure on the skin to a minimum [31].
                                               After the scan, an analysis was carried out off line by means of a custom-made image pro-
                                           cessing routine developed in Matlab 2016a software, (The Mathworks, Inc., Natick, 2016). Fas-
                                           cicle length was measured by manually outlining visible parts of muscle fascicles and the
                                           sections that were not visible were extrapolated linearly to the linearly projected line of the
                                           aponeurosis [29] (see Fig 1). The angle between the line marking the intermediate aponeurosis
                                           and the outlined fascicle was the measured, giving the PA. MT was measured as the distance
                                           between the superficial and intermediate aponeuroses.
                                               All images were collected and analyzed by the same researcher (MF), who was blinded to
                                           the identity and group of the participants during the analysis.

                                           Nordic exercise program
                                           The NHE program was performed during six weeks only in the “Nordic group”. The NHE and
                                           the program was the same as the one proposed by Petersen et al. [6], but only completed over
                                           6 weeks instead of the 10 weeks proposed in the original study. The exercise was conducted
                                           always after regular training sessions and players were supervised by their physical coach, who
                                           was informed about the exercise orally and had received written descriptions and illustrations
                                           of the exercise. Training program compliance and adverse effects were registered for each
                                           team on a weekly basis by contact with the coaches during the 6-week training period. A mini-
                                           mum of 48 h separated each training session. All training sessions were supervised by either
                                           researchers, physiotherapists or coaches.

                                           Sprint training program
                                           The sprinting program was performed only by players assigned to the “Sprint group” during
                                           six weeks with two sessions of exercises per week separated by at least 72 hours (Table 1). Each
                                           session lasted about 30–35 min and the team head coaches decided when exactly the program
                                           was performed within the training session but they were advised to follow sprint training after
                                           a proper warm-up program. The first session of the week included sprint running exercises
                                           aiming at stimulating the entire force-velocity spectrum: normal sprint accelerations (5x30 m
                                           to 3x30 m), heavy sled sprints (sled load of 70% of body mass) from 1x10 m to 3x10 m, and
                                           4x20 m (with 20 m run-up distance), and flying start sprints. The second session of the week
                                           included some ankle plantar flexors exercises with added load (from 50 to 70% body mass),
                                           unilateral bouncing exercises, plyometrics, and various athletics drills and acceleration exer-
                                           cises over short distances. All details are provided in Table 1.

                                           Soccer training program
                                           The soccer training program was performed by players assigned to all three groups during six
                                           weeks with four sessions of soccer training per week. Each session lasted about 90 minutes

621	                                                  weekly sessions of sprint training to regular soccer practice induced moderate improvements
622	                                                  in biceps femoris long head fascicle length compared to the small increases showed after iso-
623	                                                  lated eccentric strength training or not changes when practicing soccer training alone; (b)
624	                                                  biceps femoris muscle pennation angle showed a small increase only when nordic hamstring
625	                                                  exercise was added to soccer training, and not in the case of sprint training; (c) sprinting train-
626	                                                  ing added to regular soccer training produced small to large improvements in both sprint
627	                                                  acceleration performance and the underlying mechanical outputs (except maximal running
628	                                                  velocity), which contrasts with trivial or even small negative changes in the case of hamstring
629	                                                  eccentric strength training or when practicing soccer training.
630	                                                      This study is the first to explore the architectural and morphological adaptations of the
631	                                                  hamstrings in response to isolated knee flexor eccentric strength training versus sprint training
632	                                                  programmed in addition to regular soccer training during pre-season, and not in isolated con-
633	                                                  ditions without concomitant sport practice [8,11,36,37]. We think this point is an important
634	                                                  feature of the current study, since it is more in line with the real sport practice, where soccer
635	                                                  players train for soccer first, and any type of intervention is added to the basic sport practice.
636	                                                  By definition, any complementary intervention comes in addition to the main sport practice,
637	                                                  so it should not be studied separately. It is important to keep this more realistic scenario in
638	                                                  mind when discussing the results of this study and previous works, since it may influence the
639	                                                  practical conclusions of these works.

649	                                           Sprint and eccentric exercises induce changes in BFlh fascicle length
650	                                           Collectively, although our results suggest that both types of training added to soccer practice
651	                                           induced increases in the length of the fascicle BFlh, the sprint showed moderately superior
652	                                           adaptations (16%) compared to the NHE (7%). These adaptations may result from the addition
653	                                           of in-series sarcomeres [10]. It has been proposed that this increase in serial sarcomeres is asso-
654	                                           ciated with both a rightward shift in a muscle’s force-length relationship, while also reducing
655	                                           its susceptibility to damage associated with strain [10]. However, fascicle lengthening due to
656	                                           increases in tendon stiffness is one possible alternative explanation [38]. Due to the limitations
657	                                           of the static method used in the present and previous studies[12,13], further research is clearly
658	                                           needed to fully understand the mechanism(s) responsible for these architectural changes (mus-
659	                                           cle-tendon interaction) and validate the suggested hypotheses in dynamic (not only isolated,
660	                                           static) actions.
661	                                               The greater increase of BFlh FL observed after a comprehensive sprinting programme com-
662	                                           pared to NHE could be related to the continuous and increased intensity lengthening of the
663	                                           muscle-tendon unit induced by high-speed movements (for exercises targeting the velocity
664	                                           end of the sprint force-velocity spectrum) and sprint-specific strength overload (for exercises
665	                                           targeting the force-end of the spectrum). Similarly, studies on the architecture of other muscle
666	                                           groups, such as the vastus lateralis reported a significant greater increase in fascicle length
667	                                           without pennation angle changes (as in the present study) after a period of sprint/jump train-
668	                                           ing alone compared to those who added different resistance training programs. [39]. Recently,
669	                                           sprint training has been shown effective for improving eccentric hamstring strength in adoles-
670	                                           cent athletes, in addition to the positive effects on sprint performance [40]. These arguments,
671	                                           among others, may partly explain recent preliminary research suggesting a protective effect of
672	                                           an adequate exposure to maximum velocity sprint efforts in different soccer codes that would
673	                                           place sprinting itself as part of a comprehensive strategy (including other evidenced strategies)
674	                                           to prevent soft-tissue injuries [41,42].
675	                                               The observed increase in BFlh fiber length at rest after NHE was added to regular soccer
676	                                           training in the present study (7%) is similar to the results found in a group of elite young
677	                                           French soccer players following an eccentric-biased hamstring training program (~ 5%) [43]
678	                                           but considerably lower than the increases (between 16–32%) observed in other studies after
679	                                           6–12 weeks of various strength training modalities (leg curl, isokinetic dynamometry and
680	                                           NHE, respectively) focused on knee flexor eccentric overload [11,36,37]. Even that architec-
681	                                           tural variables vary considerably between individuals, which may explain that the average
682	                                           changes in architectural variables differ between studies, the ultrasonography approach used
683	                                           [11,36,37,44] to extrapolate the changes in FL may also justify the large difference in FL
684	                                           changes observed between the current study and previous ones [11,36,37,44]. The static-image
685	                                           sonographic technique used to estimate the heterogeneous and non-uniform biceps femoris
686	                                           fascicle architecture presents clear limitations [12,13] that could affect the results obtained in
687	                                           studies, including the current one. Nonetheless, the method used in this study, manual linear
688	                                           extrapolation, has recently been recommended due to a lower fascicle estimation and greater
689	                                           accuracy with respect to trigonometric equation methods used in other studies if only conven-
690	                                           tional ultrasound imaging is available [30]. Thus, on this specific point, the present results, as
691	                                           those of previous studies, should be taken with caution until more research on the improve-
692	                                           ment of ultrasonographic approach for fascicle length measurement is available.
693	                                               The discrepancy in results could also be related to the possibility that, in contrast with the
694	                                           more realistic training integrated to the usual soccer practice proposed in the present study
695	                                           [43,45], other studies included isolated eccentric training contractions targeting an increase in
696	                                           fascicle length, but not concomitant with the usual soccer practice, and the associated specific

                                           Results
                                           Mean ± SD values for all sprint performance and mechanical variables pre- and post-training
                                           intervention are shown for all groups in Table 2, along with within-group changes qualitative
                                           inferences (Table 3). Substantial differences were found in mechanical sprint variables in the
                                           “sprint group” with small to large changes with a very likely inference for all the mechanical
                                           outputs except for v0 (possibly inference). Contrastingly, these changes were less clear in “Nor-
                                           dic” and “soccer” groups, with small to trivial changes and possibly and likely inference post-
                                           training intervention.
                                               The “sprint group” showed a small increase in v0 (possibly) and RFmax (very likely), moder-
                                           ate in F0 (very likely), 5 m and 20 m times (very likely, respectively), and large in Pmax (very
                                           likely), whereas the “nordic group” showed changes ranging between small and very large
                                           increase interaction (Table 3). Trivial and unclear changes were observed in most of the sprint
                                           mechanical variables analyzed between “sprint group” and “soccer group” except for v0 and
                                           Pmax with small and moderate changes observed. Similar changes were observed between
                                           “Nordic” and “soccer” groups with small changes in v0, RFmax and 20 m time with possibly to
                                           likely inference, and moderate changes in Pmax and 5 m time with likely inference, meanwhile
                                           a large change was observed in F0 with likely inference (Table 3, Fig 2).
                                               Furthermore, variables related to biceps femoris architecture such as fascicle length, penna-
                                           tion angle and muscle thickness pre- and post-training intervention are shown for all groups
                                           in Table 4, along with within-group changes qualitative inferences (Table 5). The ICC for vari-

                                           (0.865–0.993) for pennation angle and 0.981 (0.929–0.996) for muscle thickness. SEM ranged

                                                      This study is the first to explore the architectural and morphological adaptations of the
                                                  hamstrings in response to isolated knee flexor eccentric strength training versus sprint training
                                                  programmed in addition to regular soccer training during pre-season, and not in isolated con-
                                                  ditions without concomitant sport practice [8,11,36,37]. We think this point is an important
                                                  feature of the current study, since it is more in line with the real sport practice, where soccer
                                                  players train for soccer first, and any type of intervention is added to the basic sport practice.
                                                  By definition, any complementary intervention comes in addition to the main sport practice,
                                                  so it should not be studied separately. It is important to keep this more realistic scenario in
                                                  mind when discussing the results of this study and previous works, since it may influence the

                                           Collectively, although our results suggest that both types of training added to soccer practice
                                           induced increases in the length of the fascicle BFlh, the sprint showed moderately superior
                                           adaptations (16%) compared to the NHE (7%). These adaptations may result from the addition
                                           of in-series sarcomeres [10]. It has been proposed that this increase in serial sarcomeres is asso-
                                           ciated with both a rightward shift in a muscle’s force-length relationship, while also reducing
                                           its susceptibility to damage associated with strain [10]. However, fascicle lengthening due to
                                           increases in tendon stiffness is one possible alternative explanation [38]. Due to the limitations
                                           of the static method used in the present and previous studies[12,13], further research is clearly
                                           needed to fully understand the mechanism(s) responsible for these architectural changes (mus-
                                           cle-tendon interaction) and validate the suggested hypotheses in dynamic (not only isolated,
                                           static) actions.
                                               The greater increase of BFlh FL observed after a comprehensive sprinting programme com-
                                           pared to NHE could be related to the continuous and increased intensity lengthening of the
                                           muscle-tendon unit induced by high-speed movements (for exercises targeting the velocity
                                           end of the sprint force-velocity spectrum) and sprint-specific strength overload (for exercises
                                           targeting the force-end of the spectrum). Similarly, studies on the architecture of other muscle
                                           groups, such as the vastus lateralis reported a significant greater increase in fascicle length
                                           without pennation angle changes (as in the present study) after a period of sprint/jump train-
                                           ing alone compared to those who added different resistance training programs. [39]. Recently,
                                           sprint training has been shown effective for improving eccentric hamstring strength in adoles-
                                           cent athletes, in addition to the positive effects on sprint performance [40]. These arguments,
                                           among others, may partly explain recent preliminary research suggesting a protective effect of
                                           an adequate exposure to maximum velocity sprint efforts in different soccer codes that would
                                           place sprinting itself as part of a comprehensive strategy (including other evidenced strategies)
                                           to prevent soft-tissue injuries [41,42].
                                               The observed increase in BFlh fiber length at rest after NHE was added to regular soccer
                                           training in the present study (7%) is similar to the results found in a group of elite young
                                           French soccer players following an eccentric-biased hamstring training program (~ 5%) [43]
                                           but considerably lower than the increases (between 16–32%) observed in other studies after
                                           6–12 weeks of various strength training modalities (leg curl, isokinetic dynamometry and
                                           NHE, respectively) focused on knee flexor eccentric overload [11,36,37]. Even that architec-
                                           tural variables vary considerably between individuals, which may explain that the average
                                           changes in architectural variables differ between studies, the ultrasonography approach used
                                           [11,36,37,44] to extrapolate the changes in FL may also justify the large difference in FL
                                           changes observed between the current study and previous ones [11,36,37,44]. The static-image
                                           sonographic technique used to estimate the heterogeneous and non-uniform biceps femoris
                                           fascicle architecture presents clear limitations [12,13] that could affect the results obtained in
                                           studies, including the current one. Nonetheless, the method used in this study, manual linear
                                           extrapolation, has recently been recommended due to a lower fascicle estimation and greater
                                           accuracy with respect to trigonometric equation methods used in other studies if only conven-
                                           tional ultrasound imaging is available [30]. Thus, on this specific point, the present results, as

711	                                           the case in real training contexts.
712	                                               Fascicle lengthening is one possible mechanism by which the NHE and other eccentric or
713	                                           long-length hamstring exercises have been proven effective on hamstring injury reduction.
714	                                           Timmins et al. [11] recently showed, prospectively, that professional soccer players with aver-
715	                                           age BFlh fascicle length <10.56 cm were *4 times more likely to suffer a hamstring strain
716	                                           than athletes with longer fascicle length and that the probability of injury was overall estimated
717	                                           to decrease by *74% on average for every 0.5 cm increase in fascicle length. In the current
718	                                           study, we observed increases in BFlh fascicle length of *0.7 cm after Nordic and *1.6 cm
719	                                           after Sprint training programs added to the regular soccer practice. This would, according to
720	                                           the proportions described earlier, likely result in a higher reduction in hamstring injury risk
721	                                           after Sprint than Nordic interventions. However, although theoretically longer fascicles may
722	                                           enhance sprint performance by altering the operating range of muscles and increasing muscle
723	                                           force-generating capacity, only the Sprint intervention induced clear improvements in sprint
724	                                           performance and mechanics, which was not the case of the Nordic training program, as dis-
725	                                           cussed below.
726	                                               Regarding BFlh pennation angle, this study confirms previous findings by Lovell et al. [45]
727	                                           showing that the addition of knee flexor eccentric training through NHE post soccer training
728	                                           resulted in a similar hypertrophic response, identified by an increased pennation angle and
729	                                           muscle thickness (PA ~10%). This increase is considered to represent an increase of the physi-
730	                                           ological cross-sectional area with more myofibrils in parallel, enabling the improved transmis-
731	                                           sion of force developed through the muscle-tendon unit, and in turn a higher architectural
732	                                           gear ratio [7,46]. The latter will allow the pennate biceps femoris to limit the strain experienced
733	                                           by active fascicles and provide some degree of protection during fast-velocity lengthening
734	                                           actions [46]. Mechanical tension and intramuscular metabolic stress, determine the hypertro-
735	                                           phic signal of the muscle that may be amplified (as in this study) when resistance training was
736	                                           performed following high-intensity interval and endurance training, which has also been
737	                                           shown to trigger anabolic signaling pathways and hypertrophy [7].
738

740	                                           Greater improvements of sprint performance and mechanics after sprint
741	                                           training
742	                                           Concerning the sprint mechanics and performance outcomes, the ability to produce high
743	                                           acceleration and speed is considered an important quality for performance in soccer [1].
744	                                           Although hamstrings play a role in the forward orientation of the ground reaction force, espe-
745	                                           cially at high running speed (when their torque capability and electrical activity are both con-
746	                                           sidered), the results of this study showed no benefits (and even small negative changes) of a
747	                                           NHE force program added to regular soccer practice on sprint mechanical outputs and perfor-
748	                                           mance. This is consistent with previous results [14], and contrasts with two very similar recent
749	                                           studies reporting small to moderate improvements (with high inter-individual variability) in
750	                                           sprint performance after NHE training in a group of soccer players [15,16]. Although sprint
751	                                           acceleration mechanical properties were not analyzed in these studies [15,16], the time of reali-
752	                                           zation of the program (pre-season versus in-season), and match and training high running
753	                                           speed exposure, internal and external training load may explain the differences between stud-
754	                                           ies. Ishøi et al. [15] reported concomitant average group changes, but not the direct

764	                                           performance. Furthermore, previous studies [14] reported substantial increases in hamstring
765	                                           strength with no or minimal concomitant changes in sprint acceleration mechanical outputs
766	                                           and performance. These two facts clearly question the idea that isolated posterior thigh
767	                                           strengthening alone (using for example the NHE modality) directly results in the improvement
768	                                           of such a complex neuromuscular task as maximal sprint acceleration, despite the fact that
769	                                           hamstring muscles play a role, especially when taking their sprint-specific activity as derived
770	                                           from electromyographical analysis [17]. This is not surprising given the large differences in the
771	                                           timing, velocity, length, hip-knee kinematics and overall intra- and inter-muscles coordination
772	                                           between any isolated hamstring strengthening exercise (a fortiori a single-joint, bilateral one
773	                                           like the NHE) and the sprint acceleration tasks.
774	                                               In contrast, the specific comprehensive sprint program used in the present study resulted in
775	                                           moderate and very likely improvements on both sprint mechanics (mainly acceleration vari-
776	                                           ables) and performance after 6 weeks during soccer preseason where the total workload is
777	                                           greater than in-season [47], comparatively favoring the increase of aerobic fitness to the detri-
778	                                           ment of anaerobic capacity [48]. Specifically, this program (likely due to the use of resisted and
779	                                           unresisted sprints) resulted in higher maximal force output in the horizontal direction (F0 i.e.
780	                                           first meters of the acceleration phase), also evidenced by a greater RFmax. This specific vari-
781	                                           able of the sprint force-velocity profile, which was shown to markedly decrease after hamstring
782	                                           injury [18], increased here substantially in the Sprint group, whereas only a small increase was
783	                                           observed in the ability to produce horizontal force at high speeds (v0). The results of the Sprint
784	                                           group are similar to what Morin et al. [49] reported in a pilot study using very heavy sled resis-
785	                                           tance training in soccer players: specific F0 and RF Max improvements with only trivial effect
786	                                           on v0, and only trivial changes in the control group who performed unresisted sprints. Inter-
787	                                           estingly, this brings support to the use of a comprehensive sprint training that (a) covers/stim-
788	                                           ulate a large spectrum of force and velocity conditions (ranging from heavy resistance to flying
789	                                           start sprints) and (b) uses acceleration athletics drills and horizontal plyometric exercises. We
790	                                           think that this represents a more comprehensive (thus potentially more effective) overload
791	                                           than using unresisted sprints alone. Furthermore, soccer practice itself already includes unre-
792	                                           sisted, “classical” sprints, by definition. Our results suggest that this type of multifaceted
793	                                           sprint-specific program is effective to counteract the decrease in F0 observed after soccer pre-
794	                                           season [50] or hamstring injury [18]. Although it is still a hypothesis, a reverse thinking would
795	                                           make this increase in maximal sprint force output potentially beneficial in the return-to-per-
796	                                           formance, or even prevention process. This should be the topic of future studies, but it makes
797	                                           sense in light of the data previously published on the topic and the current results.
798	                                               Some limitations associated with this manuscript should be acknowledged. No collection of
799	                                           match and training exposure, internal and external training load variables was performed dur-
800	                                           ing the study. Although all these variables were likely very similar among players, they are pos-
801	                                           sibly confounding factors of fascicle length adaptation. With that being said, the present study
802	                                           is, to our knowledge, the first to integrate and compare, within the same randomized con-
803	                                           trolled protocol, a commonly used injury prevention method (using an isolated, single-joint
804	                                           hamstring strength exercise, NHE), and a comprehensive training program specifically target-
805	                                           ing sprinting performance (through stimulation of the entire force-velocity spectrum) in a
806	                                           realistic soccer practice context.
807	                                               Secondly, the use of two-dimensional ultrasound to estimate fascicle length, although previ-
808	                                           ously validated against cadaveric measurements [51], has some associated methodological lim-

810	                                           width resulting in a greater fascicle estimations, restricted region of interest analyzed, ques-

                                           to decrease by *74% on average for every 0.5 cm increase in fascicle length. In the current
                                           study, we observed increases in BFlh fascicle length of *0.7 cm after Nordic and *1.6 cm
                                           after Sprint training programs added to the regular soccer practice. This would, according to
                                           the proportions described earlier, likely result in a higher reduction in hamstring injury risk
                                           after Sprint than Nordic interventions. However, although theoretically longer fascicles may
                                           enhance sprint performance by altering the operating range of muscles and increasing muscle
                                           force-generating capacity, only the Sprint intervention induced clear improvements in sprint
                                           performance and mechanics, which was not the case of the Nordic training program, as dis-
                                           cussed below.
                                               Regarding BFlh pennation angle, this study confirms previous findings by Lovell et al. [45]
                                           showing that the addition of knee flexor eccentric training through NHE post soccer training
                                           resulted in a similar hypertrophic response, identified by an increased pennation angle and
                                           muscle thickness (PA ~10%). This increase is considered to represent an increase of the physi-
                                           ological cross-sectional area with more myofibrils in parallel, enabling the improved transmis-
                                           sion of force developed through the muscle-tendon unit, and in turn a higher architectural
                                           gear ratio [7,46]. The latter will allow the pennate biceps femoris to limit the strain experienced
                                           by active fascicles and provide some degree of protection during fast-velocity lengthening
                                           actions [46]. Mechanical tension and intramuscular metabolic stress, determine the hypertro-
                                           phic signal of the muscle that may be amplified (as in this study) when resistance training was
                                           performed following high-intensity interval and endurance training, which has also been
                                           shown to trigger anabolic signaling pathways and hypertrophy [7].


                                           Greater improvements of sprint performance and mechanics after sprint
                                           training
                                           Concerning the sprint mechanics and performance outcomes, the ability to produce high
                                           acceleration and speed is considered an important quality for performance in soccer [1].
                                           Although hamstrings play a role in the forward orientation of the ground reaction force, espe-
                                           cially at high running speed (when their torque capability and electrical activity are both con-
                                           sidered), the results of this study showed no benefits (and even small negative changes) of a
                                           NHE force program added to regular soccer practice on sprint mechanical outputs and perfor-
                                           mance. This is consistent with previous results [14], and contrasts with two very similar recent
                                           studies reporting small to moderate improvements (with high inter-individual variability) in
                                           sprint performance after NHE training in a group of soccer players [15,16]. Although sprint
                                           acceleration mechanical properties were not analyzed in these studies [15,16], the time of reali-
                                           zation of the program (pre-season versus in-season), and match and training high running
                                           speed exposure, internal and external training load may explain the differences between stud-
                                           ies. Ishøi et al. [15] reported concomitant average group changes, but not the direct



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0228283 February 11, 2020                                                                     14 / 19
                                                                                 Architectural and performance effects of different training programs



                                           association, on an individual basis, between improvements in knee flexors strength and sprint
                                           performance. Furthermore, previous studies [14] reported substantial increases in hamstring
                                           strength with no or minimal concomitant changes in sprint acceleration mechanical outputs
                                           and performance. These two facts clearly question the idea that isolated posterior thigh
                                           strengthening alone (using for example the NHE modality) directly results in the improvement
                                           of such a complex neuromuscular task as maximal sprint acceleration, despite the fact that
                                           hamstring muscles play a role, especially when taking their sprint-specific activity as derived
                                           from electromyographical analysis [17]. This is not surprising given the large differences in the
                                           timing, velocity, length, hip-knee kinematics and overall intra- and inter-muscles coordination
                                           between any isolated hamstring strengthening exercise (a fortiori a single-joint, bilateral one
                                           like the NHE) and the sprint acceleration tasks.
                                               In contrast, the specific comprehensive sprint program used in the present study resulted in
                                           moderate and very likely improvements on both sprint mechanics (mainly acceleration vari-
                                           ables) and performance after 6 weeks during soccer preseason where the total workload is
                                           greater than in-season [47], comparatively favoring the increase of aerobic fitness to the detri-
                                           ment of anaerobic capacity [48]. Specifically, this program (likely due to the use of resisted and
                                           unresisted sprints) resulted in higher maximal force output in the horizontal direction (F0 i.e.
                                           first meters of the acceleration phase), also evidenced by a greater RFmax. This specific vari-
                                           able of the sprint force-velocity profile, which was shown to markedly decrease after hamstring
                                           injury [18], increased here substantially in the Sprint group, whereas only a small increase was
                                           observed in the ability to produce horizontal force at high speeds (v0). The results of the Sprint
                                           group are similar to what Morin et al. [49] reported in a pilot study using very heavy sled resis-
                                           tance training in soccer players: specific F0 and RF Max improvements with only trivial effect
                                           on v0, and only trivial changes in the control group who performed unresisted sprints. Inter-
                                           estingly, this brings support to the use of a comprehensive sprint training that (a) covers/stim-
                                           ulate a large spectrum of force and velocity conditions (ranging from heavy resistance to flying
                                           start sprints) and (b) uses acceleration athletics drills and horizontal plyometric exercises. We
                                           think that this represents a more comprehensive (thus potentially more effective) overload
                                           than using unresisted sprints alone. Furthermore, soccer practice itself already includes unre-
                                           sisted, “classical” sprints, by definition. Our results suggest that this type of multifaceted
                                           sprint-specific program is effective to counteract the decrease in F0 observed after soccer pre-
                                           season [50] or hamstring injury [18]. Although it is still a hypothesis, a reverse thinking would
                                           make this increase in maximal sprint force output potentially beneficial in the return-to-per-
                                           formance, or even prevention process. This should be the topic of future studies, but it makes
                                           sense in light of the data previously published on the topic and the current results.
                                               Some limitations associated with this manuscript should be acknowledged. No collection of
                                           match and training exposure, internal and external training load variables was performed dur-
                                           ing the study. Although all these variables were likely very similar among players, they are pos-
                                           sibly confounding factors of fascicle length adaptation. With that being said, the present study
                                           is, to our knowledge, the first to integrate and compare, within the same randomized con-
                                           trolled protocol, a commonly used injury prevention method (using an isolated, single-joint
                                           hamstring strength exercise, NHE), and a comprehensive training program specifically target-
                                           ing sprinting performance (through stimulation of the entire force-velocity spectrum) in a
                                           realistic soccer practice context.
                                               Secondly, the use of two-dimensional ultrasound to estimate fascicle length, although previ-
                                           ously validated against cadaveric measurements [51], has some associated methodological lim-
                                           itations mainly derived from a reduced field of view as a consequence of a too small transducer
                                           width resulting in a greater fascicle estimations, restricted region of interest analyzed, ques-
                                           tionable mathematical extrapolations and omission of fascicle and aponeurosis 3-dimensional



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0228283 February 11, 2020                                                                    15 / 19
                                                                                 Architectural and performance effects of different training programs



                                           curvature [12,30,52,53]. Moreover, the fact that the assessment method is based on 2-dimen-
                                           sional static measurement conditions limits its extrapolation to dynamic tasks. Future research
                                           should consider the use of extended field of view ultrasonography and 3-dimensional measure-
                                           ments to minimize potential error and take into account fascicle rotation during dynamic con-
                                           ditions, beyond resting, static conditions [51–53]. Finally, we could not assess the hamstring
                                           force output in the current study (via for example isokinetic or Nordic exercise testing), but a
                                           recent study showed that a sprint program induced some positive changes in both sprint per-
                                           formance and hamstring eccentric strength output as measured during the Nordic exercise in
                                           young athletes [40].

    Conclusions
    Assuming fascicle length as a factor to be considered in the management of hamstring strain
    injuries, adding a sprint-focused program to regular soccer training induced greater increases
    in biceps femoris fascicle length than incorporation of Nordic hamstring exercise as a comple-
    mentary intervention during the first 6 week of preseason period, compared with soccer prac-
    tice alone. However, only the sprint comprehensive training provided this potentially
    preventive stimulus (increase fascicle length), and at the same time induced better sprint per-
    formance and mechanical outcomes, which could be considered a practical “win-win” strategy
    for the management of hamstring injuries. Due to the specificity of sprint training and low
    cost of testing methods (all variables can now be derived from split times or slow-motion vid-
    eos with a validated App [54] of the sprints and online free computation spreadsheets (https://
    www.researchgate.net/publication/321767606_Spreadsheet_for_Sprint_acceleration_force-
    velocity-power_profiling), both players and staff can be more compliant to this type of inter-
    vention, compared to previously proposed methods. Finally, based on the current pilot results,
    further studies should test whether a comprehensive sprint training offers significant injury
    prevention advantages, as suggested recently [41,42].

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "Sports performance - is there evidence that the body clock plays a role.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role?') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of the time-of-day pattern in athletic performance and whether the internal body clock contributes to it. It draws on laboratory and simulated-competition studies of strength, power, running, swimming, cycling and skilled tasks. The authors report performance peaks at about 15:30 to 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean in studies that sampled at least six times across 24 hours.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search method, so the choice of studies cannot be checked. The authors note that much of the cited work is short-duration and of poor quality, and that the body clock cannot yet be separated from time awake and environmental factors.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the evening performance peak as proof that the body clock drives it, when the authors say current evidence cannot separate the body clock from sleep, time awake and environmental cues.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2009,
   "citation": "Reilly T, Waterhouse J. Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role? Eur J Appl Physiol. 2009;106:321-332.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s00421-009-1066-x",
   "abstract": "Athletic performance shows a time-of-day effect with possible causes in environmental factors, the sleep-wake cycle and the internal body clock. The authors conclude that the body clock probably plays some role in sports performance rhythms, but the evidence does not separate it from time awake. They outline protocols to separate these roles and note that muscle fatigue is a serious barrier to experimental work.",
   "tldr": "Sports performance follows a time-of-day pattern that peaks in the late afternoon, and the body clock probably contributes to it. Current evidence cannot yet say how much of the pattern is the body clock rather than time awake or the environment.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the time-of-day performance literature and chronobiological evidence, with suggested experimental protocols. No systematic search method is described.",
   "findings": "Many performance measures are higher in the late afternoon and early evening than in the morning. Reported rhythm peaks fall between about 15:30 and 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean. The authors judge that the body clock probably plays some role, but the evidence is inconclusive.",
   "limitations": "The authors describe much of the data as poor quality, and many studies compared only two times of day, so sampling was too infrequent to describe a circadian rhythm. Muscle fatigue makes rigorous protocols long or unacceptable, and the body clock and time awake cannot yet be separated.",
   "practicalImplications": "When comparing athlete performance across the day, standardise and record test times, because the time of day alone can shift results. Where possible, test protocols should separate time awake from the body clock.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance measures tend to peak in the late afternoon and early evening, so training and testing schedules could take time of day into account. This review cannot say how much of that rhythm is the body clock.",
   "rtp": "This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.limitations: 'small or unbalanced designs' is not stated in the text -> poor-quality data and too-infrequent sampling ('many have compared performances at only two times of day'; 'sampling has been too infrequent')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q06",
 "sourceFile": "Sprint running- from fundamental mechanics to practice—a review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice - a review') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Track & Field", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Invited narrative review that applies fundamental mechanical principles to sprint running research. It assesses spring-mass models, force and power analyses based on total and horizontal (end-goal) force, and common coaching concepts. The authors argue that some models and power calculations from isolated horizontal force can lead to misinterpretation.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search method, so the choice of literature cannot be checked. It is largely a theoretical argument, and its own calculations are illustrations that reuse previously published data sets rather than a new study.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat a model that fits sprint kinematics as proof of the underlying mechanism, which the authors say a model cannot establish.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Haugen T, McGhie D, Ettema G. Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice - a review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s00421-019-04139-0",
   "abstract": "The authors examine sprint running literature using the mechanical principles that govern accelerated running. They discuss spring-mass models and their limits, the link between sprint mechanics and metabolic demand, and the emphasis on total and horizontal force. They argue that power analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed and discuss some practical concepts in sprint coaching.",
   "tldr": "Sprint mechanics research can be misread when models or horizontal-force power figures are taken at face value. Coaches and analysts should check how a measure was derived before using it to explain sprint performance.",
   "methods": "Invited narrative review of sprint running mechanics literature, interpreted through fundamental mechanical principles. No systematic search method is described.",
   "findings": "Spring-mass models describe gross sprint kinematics such as step length, step rate and contact time, but the authors argue they have flaws when applied to accelerated running. Analyses based on total and horizontal force, and power derived from isolated end-goal force, are argued to be limited or flawed. Metabolic models of sprinting are described as promising but still model based.",
   "limitations": "The review is an argument rather than a systematic synthesis, and no search method is described. Its illustrative calculations use a few published data sets, and its views on practical sprint concepts are discussed rather than tested.",
   "practicalImplications": "Check how a sprint model or force measure was derived before treating it as a mechanism. Interpret horizontal-force power figures obtained from isolated force data with caution.",
   "athleteDev": "The authors suggest that sprint conditioning in most well-trained senior sprinters should target step rate, which they describe as the main within-athlete speed modulator, while longer step length, which requires strength, separates fast from intermediate sprinters. Model-based power figures should not be read as direct measures of an athlete's capacity.",
   "rtp": "This review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria."
 },

  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "sourceFile: restored the exact inputs.json string (non-breaking spaces and dash) that the draft had normalised",

   "screeningLimitations/limitations: 'reports no new athlete data' -> its own calculations reuse previously published data sets (e.g. 'We calculated leg stiffness for our own data (national level sprinters)')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Online-first version: only the 2019 copyright and received/accepted dates are printed, with no volume, issue or pages.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

 "id": "Q07",
 "sourceFile": "Sprint vs isolated eccentric training - Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text ('Sprint versus isolated eccentric training: Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players') matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Healthy Athletes", "Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Soccer players from an elite regional division were randomly assigned within matched pairs to a sprint group, a Nordic hamstring exercise group or a soccer-only group for the six preseason weeks; 32 were recruited and 23 completed (8 sprint, 7 Nordic, 8 soccer-only). The sprint group showed small to large within-group improvements in sprint acceleration performance (5 m and 20 m times) and mechanical outputs, except only a small gain in maximal velocity, and a moderate increase in biceps femoris long head fascicle length, compared with a smaller increase in the Nordic group. Only the Nordic group showed a small increase in pennation angle.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Very small analysed groups (7 to 8 per group), with no record of match or training load, and two-dimensional ultrasound estimates of fascicle length that the authors note have known limits. Between-group sprint differences versus soccer-only were mostly trivial or unclear, and injury was not measured.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the fascicle-length gain as proof that sprint training prevents hamstring injury, when the study measured muscle architecture and sprint performance only.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Mendiguchia J, Conceição F, Edouard P, Fonseca M, Pereira R, Lopes H, et al. Sprint versus isolated eccentric training: Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players. PLoS ONE. 2020;15(2):e0228283.",
   "doi": "10.1371/journal.pone.0228283",
   "abstract": "The study compared Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint training, both added to regular soccer practice, on sprint performance, sprint mechanics and biceps femoris long head architecture. Six preseason weeks were compared across a soccer-only group, a Nordic group and a sprint group. The authors conclude that sprint training increased fascicle length more than Nordic training and also improved sprint performance and mechanics, while Nordic training did not improve sprint performance.",
   "tldr": "Adding sprint training to a soccer preseason improved short sprint times and acceleration mechanics and increased hamstring fascicle length in this small sample. Injury protection was not measured, so the fascicle result should not be read as injury prevention.",
   "methods": "Prospective randomised controlled study over six preseason weeks in 32 recruited soccer players who were allocated to three groups, with matching by position, playing status and previous hamstring injury. Nine players dropped out, leaving 23 analysed. Outcomes were 5 m and 20 m times and force-velocity mechanical outputs (F0, v0, Pmax, RFmax) from radar-measured 50 m sprints, and biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness by two-dimensional ultrasound, analysed with magnitude-based inference.",
   "findings": "In the sprint group, sprint performance and mechanics showed small to large pre-post improvements, with only a small, possibly real gain in maximal velocity (v0). The sprint group showed a moderate increase in fascicle length (about 16 percent), compared with a smaller increase in the Nordic group (about 7 percent) and a trivial change in the soccer-only group. The soccer-only and Nordic groups showed trivial to small negative sprint changes, and only the Nordic group showed a small increase in pennation angle.",
   "limitations": "Only 23 of 32 players were analysed, and the abstract reports the group sizes at recruitment (10, 12 and 10). Training and match load were not recorded, two-dimensional ultrasound has known limits for fascicle estimates, and injury outcomes were not measured. Between-group sprint comparisons with the soccer-only group were mostly trivial or unclear, and results rely on magnitude-based inference rather than hypothesis tests.",
   "practicalImplications": "Sprint work within preseason soccer practice may improve short sprint times and acceleration mechanics over six weeks. Staff should not replace Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint work on the basis of this study, because injury protection was not tested.",
   "athleteDev": "In this sample, sprint training within routine soccer practice improved 5 m and 20 m times and acceleration mechanics over six preseason weeks. Its effect on biceps femoris long head fascicle length was larger than that of the Nordic group.",
   "rtp": "The study excluded players with recent hip, knee or lumbo-pelvic joint injury, used previous hamstring injury only as a matching variable, and did not measure return to play. It cannot show how sprint or Nordic training should guide return-to-sport decisions after a hamstring injury."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/tldr/practicalImplications/athleteDev: '50 m sprint performance' -> 5 m and 20 m times and acceleration mechanics (50 m was the test distance; 'sprint performance was described via the measurement of 5 m (s) and 20 m (s) times')",
   "paper.rtp: 'players without recent hamstring injury' -> exclusion covered hip, knee or lumbo-pelvic joint injury, and previous hamstring injury was a matching variable ('matched depending on their position ..., playing status ..., and previous hamstring injury')",
   "screeningLimitations/limitations: added that between-group sprint changes versus soccer-only were mostly trivial or unclear (Table 3: F0 0.07, RFmax 0.01, 5 m 0.11 'Trivial') and that magnitude-based inference was used",
   "populations: Mixed / Unspecified -> Professional / Elite (players from 'the same Elite Division of Football Association of Porto')",
